warmup.q: On an 8-core machine running JDK 21, a shop's program calls CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> bank.charge(card)) with no pool. Where does the 200 ms call to the bank run?
options: On the thread that called supplyAsync, a little later
On a virtual thread created for the call
On a worker of ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which the whole JVM shares
On a new thread created for the call
warmup.why: With no pool, the async methods use the common pool, one pool that every parallel stream in the JVM uses too. On 8 cores it has 7 threads. A new thread per task only happened on JDK 21 to 24 when the common pool had fewer than 2 threads, as in a container with 2 CPUs, and JDK 25 removed even that. You get a virtual thread only if you pass a virtual-thread executor. The first section shows the thread names.

opening:
Picture a busy kitchen and an order for table 4: steak with pepper sauce. The steak goes on the grill and the sauce on the stove, at the same time. The order's ticket carries instructions: "When the steak and the sauce are both ready, plate them and send them to table 4."

Nobody stands at the grill watching the steak. (It cooks just as fast without an audience.) Whichever cook finishes the last part reads the ticket and does the next step.

The tickets from the last two lessons couldn't carry instructions. A Future could only be waited on or read, and every wait held a thread, a path of work, doing nothing. Java's CompletableFuture is a ticket that can.

The new ticket has two easy traps. A chain of steps can look side by side and still run one after another. Or it can run on a pool the whole program shares, where one slow call holds up strangers. Both pass every test.

In this lesson, we'll rebuild the shop's checkout with these tickets, see which thread runs each step, and decide where waiting is still allowed. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a ticket for table 4 that carried its own instructions: when the steak and the sauce are ready, plate them. CompletableFuture is that ticket. We started the price and the rate side by side and joined them. Then we watched a chain that looked just as quick take twice as long, and found that whichever thread finishes a stage carries the next step.

Now search your own code for supplyAsync( and runAsync( with a single argument. Each one should be short computing work, or get a pool.

Next, we'll let a station fail. When the steak burns at the grill, or the rate service throws, which steps still run, and how do we put a time limit on the whole order?

sections.h: A ticket that knows the next step: CompletableFuture, and the pool that runs it
sections.html:
Back to the shop's checkout. The shop prices everything in euros, and an American customer pays in dollars.

So the checkout needs two answers from two slow services. The cart service knows the cart's price in euros. The rate service knows the exchange rate, how many dollars one euro buys. (The code calls it fx, short for foreign exchange.) Each takes 300 ms. Then the checkout multiplies the two and charges the card.

Here's the honest version, with the tickets from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption. io is a thread pool, a small team of threads that take tasks from a queue:

Java
Future<BigDecimal> price = io.submit(() -> prices.priceEur(cart));
Future<BigDecimal> rate = io.submit(() -> fx.rate("EUR", "USD"));
BigDecimal usd = price.get().multiply(rate.get());   // this thread waits here, doing nothing
Kotlin
val price = io.submit<BigDecimal> { prices.priceEur(cart) }
val rate = io.submit<BigDecimal> { fx.rate("EUR", "USD") }
val usd = price.get() * rate.get()                    // this thread waits here, doing nothing

Credit where it's due: it's correct, and both calls run side by side, so the wait is 300 ms, not 600. The catch is the thread that calls get(). It sits there for the whole 300 ms, doing nothing. Little's law, from Sizing a pool, says the number inside equals the arrival rate times the time each one stays. At 400 checkouts a second, that's 400 x 0.3 = 120 threads, all just waiting.

A CompletableFuture<T> is a ticket you can clip instructions to. It's still a Future, so get and cancel still work. But it also lets you say "when this is done, do that next", and walk away.

Something has to complete the ticket, and usually that's supplyAsync. (Async is short for asynchronous: the work runs while your code moves on.) It takes a Supplier, a function that takes nothing and returns a value. It runs the supplier on the pool you name, and completes the ticket with the result:

Java
CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cart), io);   // starts now, on io
CompletableFuture<Void> note =
        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> orderLog.write(cart), io);       // no result
Kotlin
val price: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cart) }, io)      // starts now, on io
val note: CompletableFuture<Void> =
    CompletableFuture.runAsync({ orderLog.write(cart) }, io)          // no result

Both calls return at once, while the work runs on io or waits in its queue. runAsync is the same for a task with no result. A ticket can also be completed by hand: a library can hand you a new CompletableFuture<>() and call complete(value) on it when its answer arrives. The payment service in this lesson's lab, the service that charges the card, works that way. The lab calls its client PaymentGateway, and its charge method returns a ticket.

The second argument, the pool, matters more than it looks. Leave it out, and the task goes to the default async executor, ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). That's one pool per JVM, the program that runs your Java code. It has one thread fewer than the machine has cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time.

Every parallel stream (a stream that splits its work across threads) uses it, and so does every library that calls supplyAsync without a pool. It's the shared kitchen that everyone borrows and nobody owns. A few 300 ms calls fill it, and everyone else's work waits behind them.

WhoRunsItDemo, in the Try it below, prints the thread that runs each supplyAsync, first without a pool and then with a pool named io. On a 4-core machine with JDK 21:

JDK 21, common pool parallelism 3
supplyAsync(task)      ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
supplyAsync(task)      ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
supplyAsync(task)      ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
supplyAsync(task, io)  ran on io-1
supplyAsync(task, io)  ran on io-2
supplyAsync(task, io)  ran on io-2

The version of the JDK, Java's standard library and tools, changes the small-machine case. Many programs run in a container, a fenced-off space where the operating system limits how much CPU a program may use. In a container limited to 2 CPUs, the common pool gets just one thread. Up to JDK 24, CompletableFuture noticed that and skipped the pool: it started a brand-new thread for every task. JDK 25 removed that special case.

Run the demo with 1cpu, which sizes the common pool as that container would, and the two versions disagree. JDK 21 runs the three calls on Thread-0, Thread-1 and Thread-2, a new thread each time. JDK 25 runs all three on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1. For a call that waits, both are wrong: one has no limit, and the other has a limit of one.

Without a pool, async work runs on threads the whole JVM shares. Pass a pool for anything that waits.

The pool you pass can be a fixed pool sized the way Sizing a pool showed. On JDK 21 and later, it can also be Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), which gives each task a virtual thread, a much lighter kind of thread that a later track covers. Keep the default for short computing work.

The price and the rate are on their way. Now we clip on the instructions.

try.title: Find out who runs your task
steps: Run WhoRunsItDemo. Note the thread names with and without a pool.
Run it again with -Pargs=1cpu, which sizes the common pool as a 2-CPU container would. Predict the names first. Does your JDK version change the answer?

code.title: WhoRunsItDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; /** Which thread runs supplyAsync? Pass "1cpu" to size the common pool the way a 2-CPU container does. */ public class WhoRunsItDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("1cpu")) { // must run before anything touches ForkJoinPool: a 2-CPU container gets parallelism 1 System.setProperty("java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism", "1"); } System.out.println("JDK " + Runtime.version().feature() + ", common pool parallelism " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task) ran on " + who); } try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName(), io).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task, io) ran on " + who); } } } }

sections.h: Clipping on instructions: thenApply maps, thenCompose flattens, thenCombine waits for two
sections.html:
Each of these methods takes a ticket, clips on one instruction, and hands back a new ticket for that instruction's result. Here's the smallest one, on a ticket that is already complete:

Java
CompletableFuture<Integer> six = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(6);
CompletableFuture<Integer> answer = six.thenApply(n -> n * 7);   // a new ticket, for 42
Kotlin
val six = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(6)
val answer = six.thenApply { n -> n * 7 }                         // a new ticket, for 42

Each step is called a stage: a ticket, plus the instruction that completes it from earlier results. Which method you use depends on the shape of the instruction you have:

You have Method You get
T -> U, plain code thenApply CompletableFuture<U>
T -> CompletableFuture<U>, another async call thenCompose CompletableFuture<U>
a second ticket, and (T, U) -> V thenCombine CompletableFuture<V>
T -> void, a side effect thenAccept CompletableFuture<Void>

thenCompose needs a second look. Say a step calls the payment service, which already returns its own ticket. With thenApply, you'd get a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<String>>: a ticket for a ticket, and nobody collects the inner one. thenCompose flattens it into a single CompletableFuture<String>. (If you know Optional or streams: thenApply is map, and thenCompose is flatMap.)

Now the checkout. CombineDemo starts the price and the rate, joins them with thenCombine, and logs each event with its time and thread. Here's the heart of it:

Java
// both calls start now and run side by side
CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io);
CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io);
usd = price.thenCombine(rate, BigDecimal::multiply);
Kotlin
// both calls start now and run side by side
val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::priceEur, io)
val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::eurToUsd, io)
price.thenCombine(rate) { p, r -> p * r }

Read the last line as the ticket for table 4: when the price and the rate are both ready, multiply them. Each call takes 300 ms, so I expect the charge a little after 300 ms. On a busy machine:

  36 ms  main   pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet
 330 ms  io-1   price is 100.00 EUR
 332 ms  io-2   rate is 1.0842
 347 ms  main   charge 108.42 USD

The run matched my guess. The main thread built the whole pipeline in 36 ms and walked away. The price and the rate arrived together, on two io threads, and the charge followed.

Now a setback. The chain version fetches the rate inside thenCompose, after the price arrives:

Java
// the rate call starts only when the price has arrived
usd = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io)
        .thenCompose(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io)
                .thenApply(p::multiply));
Kotlin
// the rate call starts only when the price has arrived
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::priceEur, io)
    .thenCompose { p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::eurToUsd, io).thenApply { r -> p * r } }

The chain is just as asynchronous, and main still walks away at once. But look at the times:

  36 ms  main   pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet
 340 ms  io-1   price is 100.00 EUR
 644 ms  io-2   rate is 1.0842
 661 ms  main   charge 108.42 USD

The rate arrived at 644 ms, not 332. Nothing warned us. Both versions are asynchronous; only one of them is also fast.

The difference is where supplyAsync is called. Work starts when you call supplyAsync, not when you call thenCombine. In the first version, both calls start on the first two lines, before any instruction is clipped on. In the second, the rate call sits inside an instruction, and an instruction runs only when the stage before it completes.

Work starts when you call supplyAsync. Start everything independent first, then combine.

The figure shows where the lab takes this checkout: the charge clipped on with thenCompose, and the receipt with thenApply. If any step fails, the steps after it are skipped, and the last ticket fails with that exception. That's the next lesson.

One question is still open from the first run. The main thread built the pipeline and walked away, so which thread did the multiply?

Pass "chain" to fetch them one after the other. */ public class CombineDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-6s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } static BigDecimal priceEur() { sleep(300); // the cart service log("price is 100.00 EUR"); return new BigDecimal("100.00"); } static BigDecimal eurToUsd() { sleep(300); // the exchange-rate service log("rate is 1.0842"); return new BigDecimal("1.0842"); } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean chain = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("chain"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> usd; if (chain) { // the rate call starts only when the price has arrived usd = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io) .thenCompose(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io) .thenApply(p::multiply)); } else { // both calls start now and run side by side CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io); CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io); usd = price.thenCombine(rate, BigDecimal::multiply); } log("pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet"); log("charge " + usd.join().setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) + " USD"); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

sections.h: Who carries the order to the next station: the thread that runs each step
sections.html:
thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine and thenAccept take no pool. So who runs the instruction?

There are two cases. If the stage before it is still running when you clip the instruction on, the instruction runs on the thread that completes that stage. If that stage is already complete, the instruction runs right away, on the thread that called thenApply.

Both cases follow from one detail of the class. Each CompletableFuture keeps a stack of the instructions clipped onto it. The thread that completes the ticket, by returning from a supplyAsync task or by calling complete, then takes those instructions off one by one. It runs every one that has no pool of its own. An instruction clipped on after that finds a finished ticket, so thenApply runs it on the spot.

The kitchen from the opening works the same way: whichever cook finishes the last part reads the ticket and does the next step. So in CombineDemo, the multiply ran on whichever io thread finished second, not on main.

WhichThreadDemo shows both cases, plus the two Async variants you'll meet in a moment. Write down your guess for each line before you read on:

1. thenApply on a finished future:    main
2. thenApply attached while running:  io-1
3. thenApplyAsync(fn):                ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu):           cpu-1

Line 1 was clipped onto a finished ticket, so main ran it on the spot. Line 2 was clipped onto a ticket whose task was still sleeping on io-1, so io-1 ran it when the task finished.

For cheap steps, that's exactly right, and it's what the plain methods are for. Multiplying a price by a rate takes microseconds. It doesn't matter which thread does it, and skipping a trip to another pool saves a queue and a thread switch.

Trouble starts when the step is slow and the completing thread isn't yours. Some client libraries, the code you use to call another service, complete their tickets on a thread of their own that serves many requests at once. (That thread is often called an event loop.) A plain thenApply that blocks there for 50 ms stalls every other request it serves. The same goes for a scheduler's thread, from the last lesson, that completes a ticket at a deadline.

Here the kitchen picture breaks. A real cook who finishes the sauce knows to pass a two-hour braise to someone else. A plain thenApply doesn't. The thread that completes the stage does the next step, however slow it is, unless you name a pool.

The Async variants fix that. Every method has two of them:

  • thenApplyAsync(fn) always hands the step to the default async executor, the common pool, with the same problems as supplyAsync without a pool.
  • thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) hands it to the pool you name. Use it to move slow or waiting work off a thread you don't own.

A plain step runs on whatever thread finished the stage before. Name a pool for any step that is slow.

So far, every step completes a ticket and hands on. Sooner or later, though, somebody needs the actual value.

code.html: package workbench.executors.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** Which thread runs the next stage? It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ public class WhichThreadDemo { static String me() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()); ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x"); System.out.println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply(x -> me()).join()); CompletableFuture<String> slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(200); return "x"; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> attached = slow.thenApply(x -> me()); // attached while slow still runs System.out.println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()); System.out.println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me()).join()); System.out.println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me(), cpu).join()); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory()).use { cpu -> val done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x") println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply { me() }.join()) val slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(200); "x" }, io) val attached = slow.thenApply { me() } // attached while slow still runs println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()) println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync { me() }.join()) println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync({ me() }, cpu).join()) } } }

try.expect: main, io-1, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 and cpu-1. Line 2 runs on io-1 because the step was clipped on while the task was still sleeping, so the thread that completed it ran the step. If your machine paused main for more than 200 ms between those two lines, you'd see main there instead, which is the whole point: timing decides.

sections.h: Getting the value out: join, get, and the one place you may wait
sections.html:
Sooner or later, a thread needs the value itself. It might send a web page back to a browser, print a receipt, or check a result in a test. CompletableFuture gives you two ways to wait for it.

get() is the Future method from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption. It throws the checked exceptions InterruptedException and ExecutionException, with the failure as the cause, and get(timeout, unit) adds TimeoutException.

join() throws only unchecked exceptions: CompletionException, with the failure as the cause, or CancellationException. That makes it easy to call inside lambdas and streams. But it has no time limit, and it ignores interrupts: a thread stuck in join() stays stuck until the ticket completes. getNow(fallback) and resultNow() (JDK 19) never wait at all.

So build the whole pipeline without waiting. Then wait at most once, at the edge, on a thread that is allowed to wait, with a time limit. The edge is where your code meets the outside world, such as a request handler, the main method or a test:

Java
// a request thread that may wait, but not forever
Receipt r = checkout.checkout(cart, "USD").get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
Kotlin
// a request thread that may wait, but not forever
val r = checkout.checkout(cart, "USD").get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)

Never call join() or get() inside a stage, on a ticket that may still be running. (On a ticket you know is complete, join() returns at once.) The stage runs on a pool thread, and that thread now sits idle until another task finishes. Picture a cook who stops cooking and stands at the counter, waiting for a dish that nobody is free to cook.

A few of those, and a small pool runs out of threads. If the task being waited for is queued behind them on the same pool, nothing ever finishes. That's the pool-induced deadlock from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption, and lesson 9 of this track has you fix one. When a stage needs another async result, that's what thenCompose and thenCombine are for.

Wait once, at the edge, with a time limit. Never wait inside a stage.

The Try it below has a checkout that breaks this rule twice. Find both before you do the lab, which asks you to write it properly.

Every pipeline in this lesson has one limit: it assumes that each step succeeds, and none of its steps has a time limit. A rate service that throws, or never answers at all, needs tools we haven't met yet.

try.title: Spot the waiting calls
steps:
Read this method. Mark every line that makes a thread wait, and say which thread.

Java
CompletableFuture<Receipt> checkout(String cart) {
    BigDecimal price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cart), io).join();   // A
    CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fx.rate("EUR", "USD"), io);
    return rate.thenApply(r -> {
        BigDecimal amount = price.multiply(r);
        String id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join();                                 // B
        return new Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id);
    });
}
Kotlin
fun checkout(cart: String): CompletableFuture<Receipt> {
    val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cart) }, io).join()              // A
    val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fx.rate("EUR", "USD") }, io)
    return rate.thenApply { r ->
        val amount = price * r
        val id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join()                                     // B
        Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id)
    }
}
Sketch the fix with thenCombine and thenCompose. The lab asks you to write it for real.
try.expect: A makes the caller wait for the whole price call, and because the rate call starts only after it, the two calls run one after the other. B makes whichever thread completes rate (an io thread) wait for as long as the payment service takes. The fix starts both supplyAsync calls first, combines them with thenCombine, and calls gateway.charge inside thenCompose, so no thread waits anywhere inside checkout.

aside.title: If you write web services, do you need to wait at all?
aside.html: Often not. Many web frameworks let a request handler return a CompletionStage<T>, the interface that holds CompletableFuture's composing methods, instead of a finished value. The framework then sends the response when the stage completes, and no request thread waits in the meantime. Spring and Quarkus both work this way. If your framework offers it, return the pipeline and let the framework do the waiting.

compare.title: Two lookups side by side, then an async call

java.title: Delivery.java (CompletableFuture)
java.html: CompletableFuture<String> confirm(String orderId) { CompletableFuture<Address> address = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> customers.address(orderId), io); CompletableFuture<Duration> cooking = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> kitchen.cookTime(orderId), io); return address .thenCombine(cooking, (a, t) -> new RideRequest(a, t)) .thenCompose(riders::book) .thenApply(ride -> "Your food arrives at " + ride.eta()); }

kotlin.title: Delivery.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: suspend fun confirm(orderId: String): String = coroutineScope { val address = async(Dispatchers.IO) { customers.address(orderId) } // both start now val cooking = async(Dispatchers.IO) { kitchen.cookTime(orderId) } val request = RideRequest(address.await(), cooking.await()) val ride = riders.book(request).await() // pauses on the CompletableFuture, holds no thread "Your food arrives at ${ride.eta}" }

compare.note: The Java version is a chain of instructions: each method clips on a step, and you think about which thread runs each one. The Kotlin version reads top to bottom. It runs in coroutines, Kotlin's light tasks that can pause without holding a thread. async starts the two lookups at once, await() pauses the coroutine until a result is ready, and the await() extension from kotlinx.coroutines.future turns the rider service's CompletableFuture into a pause point. The structure differs too. If the cooking-time lookup fails, coroutineScope cancels the address lookup and rethrows. thenCombine does nothing like that: the address lookup keeps running, and its result is thrown away. The coroutines track covers the details.

worked.title: Turn a waiting delivery order into a pipeline

steps.say: A food-delivery shop confirms each order. It looks up the customer's address (40 ms) and the kitchen's cooking time (60 ms), books a delivery rider with a rider service whose client already returns a CompletableFuture (120 ms), and tells the customer when the food arrives. This version takes 40 + 60 + 120 = 220 ms per order, and holds a thread for all of it. Before reading on, mark which calls depend on which.
steps.code: String confirm(String orderId) { Address address = customers.address(orderId); // 40 ms Duration cooking = kitchen.cookTime(orderId); // 60 ms Ride ride = riders.book(new RideRequest(address, cooking)).join(); // 120 ms return "Your food arrives at " + ride.eta(); }

alt.html: fun confirm(orderId: String): String { val address = customers.address(orderId) // 40 ms val cooking = kitchen.cookTime(orderId) // 60 ms val ride = riders.book(RideRequest(address, cooking)).join() // 120 ms return "Your food arrives at ${ride.eta}" }

steps.say: The address and the cooking time don't depend on each other. The rider needs both, and the message needs the rider. So the best case is max(40, 60) + 120 = 180 ms, and only if the two lookups start together. Start both first, on the io pool, because they wait.
steps.code: // 1. start the independent lookups together CompletableFuture<Address> address = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> customers.address(orderId), io); CompletableFuture<Duration> cooking = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> kitchen.cookTime(orderId), io);

alt.html: // 1. start the independent lookups together val address = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ customers.address(orderId) }, io) val cooking = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ kitchen.cookTime(orderId) }, io)

steps.say: Join the two with thenCombine. Building the request is cheap, so the plain method is right. The rider service returns its own ticket, so flatten it with thenCompose, and finish with a cheap thenApply.
steps.code: return address .thenCombine(cooking, (a, t) -> new RideRequest(a, t)) // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(riders::book) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply(ride -> "Your food arrives at " + ride.eta()); // 4. cheap mapping

alt.html: return address .thenCombine(cooking) { a, t -> RideRequest(a, t) } // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(riders::book) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply { ride -> "Your food arrives at ${ride.eta}" } // 4. cheap mapping

steps.say: The method now returns CompletableFuture<String> and waits for nothing. The request handler that calls it waits once, with a time limit. A framework that accepts a CompletionStage gets the ticket itself instead.
steps.code: String message = confirm(orderId).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // 5. wait once, at the edge

alt.html: val message = confirm(orderId).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 5. wait once, at the edge

lab.title: Build a checkout that never waits
steps: Run the tests. All six fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read the Javadoc on Checkout.checkout: it is the spec.
Start the two slow calls first: supplyAsync for prices.priceEur(cartId) and for fx.rate("EUR", currency), both on io.
Combine them with thenCombine into the amount: price.multiply(rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN), which rounds to cents.
Charge with thenCompose, because gateway.charge (the payment service) already returns a CompletableFuture<String>. Build the Receipt from the amount and the charge ID.
Run the tests until all six pass, then run them once more.
hints: fetchesInParallel makes each call wait at a barrier until the other one arrives. If it times out, your rate call starts only after the price is back.
composesTheCharge gives the checkout an io pool with a single thread. If it fails, a stage is calling join() or get() on the payment service's ticket, and holding that thread.

The receipt needs the amount, which only exists inside the thenCompose lambda. Clip .thenApply(chargeId -> new Receipt(...)) onto the payment service's ticket inside that lambda, so amount is still in scope.

drill.title: Two lookups and a send, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write CompletableFuture<Void> sendPointsReminder(String customerId). It fetches the customer's name (customers.name(id), which waits) and their loyalty points (loyalty.points(id), which waits) side by side on io. It formats a line such as "Ana: 1250 points", and sends it with mailer.send(line), which returns a CompletableFuture<Void>. Nothing may wait. Then compare: did you start both lookups before clipping anything on?

answer.title: Reminder.java
answer.html: CompletableFuture<Void> sendPointsReminder(String customerId) { CompletableFuture<String> name = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> customers.name(customerId), io); CompletableFuture<Integer> points = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> loyalty.points(customerId), io); return name .thenCombine(points, (n, p) -> n + ": " + p + " points") // cheap, plain method .thenCompose(mailer::send); // async call, flattened }

alt.title: Reminder.kt
alt.html: fun sendPointsReminder(customerId: String): CompletableFuture<Void> { val name = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ customers.name(customerId) }, io) val points = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ loyalty.points(customerId) }, io) return name .thenCombine(points) { n, p -> "$n: $p points" } // cheap, plain method .thenCompose(mailer::send) // async call, flattened }

recap: supplyAsync(task, pool) starts work at once and returns a ticket. Without a pool, it uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which the whole JVM shares.

Up to JDK 24, a common pool with fewer than 2 threads (a container with 1 or 2 CPUs) meant a new thread per async task. From JDK 25, the common pool is always used. Pass a pool for anything that waits.
thenApply maps with plain code, thenCompose flattens a step that returns a ticket, and thenCombine waits for two tickets.
Work starts when you call supplyAsync. Start the independent calls first; a call started inside thenCompose waits for the stage before it.
A plain step runs on the thread that completes the stage before it, or on the caller if that stage is already complete. thenApplyAsync(fn, pool) moves it to your pool.
get throws the checked ExecutionException, and join the unchecked CompletionException. Wait once, at the edge, with a time limit. The limit: nothing here handles a step that fails or never finishes.

explain.prompt: A teammate wrote supplyAsync(() -> prices.price(cart)).thenCompose(p -> supplyAsync(() -> fx.rate(cur)).thenApply(p::multiply)). Explain what is slower than it needs to be, what is risky, and what you'd change.
explain.answer: It's slow because the rate call only starts inside thenCompose, after the price has come back, so the time is the sum of both calls instead of the slower one. Starting both supplyAsync calls first and joining them with thenCombine makes them overlap. It's risky because neither supplyAsync has a pool, so two calls that wait for other services run on the common pool, which has one thread fewer than the cores for the whole JVM and is shared with parallel streams. Under load they hold up everyone else, and on a small container before JDK 25 each call even gets its own new thread. I'd pass a pool meant for waiting calls, sized for the traffic, to both supplyAsync calls.

deeper.html:
The stack of instructions from the third section has one more consequence. One slow plain step delays every other plain step clipped onto the same ticket, because the completing thread runs them one after another.

CompletableFuture implements two interfaces. Future gives you get and cancel. CompletionStage has the composing methods, and nothing that completes the ticket or waits for it. When you write an API, return CompletionStage<T>, or call minimalCompletionStage() (JDK 9). Then callers can't call complete or obtrudeValue on your ticket and change a result you already computed. A caller who needs to wait can still call toCompletableFuture().join(), which makes the waiting visible in their code.

There are a few other ways to get a ticket. completedFuture(v) and failedFuture(ex) (JDK 9) are handy in tests. new CompletableFuture<>() plus complete(v) connects any library that reports its answer through a callback, a method the library calls when the answer arrives. And completeAsync(supplier, executor) (JDK 9) completes an existing ticket from a task, which helps when you must hand out the ticket before you know which pool will do the work.
